title: What to Pack for Korea's Four Seasons: A Beginner's Guide
html:
Korea has four very different seasons, and each one needs a different suitcase. Pack for the wrong season and you'll either freeze, melt in the humidity, or carry clothes you never wear. If this is your first trip to Korea, here's a simple, beginner-friendly guide to what to bring for each season — plus a few things locals do that most guidebooks skip.

Spring (March–May): layers for changeable weather

Spring in Korea is beautiful but unpredictable. Average temperatures run from about 0°C (32°F) in early March to 22°C (72°F) by May, and it can swing 10 degrees or more within a single day. Early March still feels like winter, while late April and May are pleasant and mild — this is also cherry blossom season, so parks get crowded and sunny.

  • Early spring (March): a warm coat, long pants, and a thermal (very thin, warm) layer underneath — mornings and evenings are still cold.
  • Mid-to-late spring (April–May): a light jacket or cardigan, long-sleeve shirts, and jeans. Bring a small umbrella — spring showers are common and pop up without much warning.
  • A scarf is a smart extra layer for chilly mornings in March, and you can just stuff it in your bag once it warms up.


Gyeongbokgung Palace, Seoul, late March. Photo: "Republic of Korea" (Korea.net), Wikimedia Commons, licensed CC BY-SA 2.0.

Summer (June–August): heat, humidity, and monsoon rain

Korean summers are hot and very humid, with average temperatures of 23–28°C (73–82°F) — but because of the humidity, it often feels hotter than the number suggests. From late June to late July, Korea has a rainy season called jangma (장마), when it can rain heavily for days at a time.

  • Light, breathable clothing: short sleeves, shorts, and natural fabrics like cotton or linen dry faster and feel cooler than synthetic fabrics.
  • A sturdy folding umbrella — cheap ones sold at street stalls or convenience stores often break in strong wind, so a slightly better one is worth it during jangma.
  • Waterproof shoes or sandals for rainy days, plus sunscreen and a hat or portable fan for the many sunny, humid days in between.
  • A small hand towel — many locals carry one to wipe off sweat, since public restrooms don't always have paper towels or hand dryers.


An umbrella is essential during Korea's summer rainy season. Photo: Don O'Brien, Wikimedia Commons, licensed CC BY 2.0.

Autumn (September–November): the easiest season to pack for

Many travelers — and locals — say autumn is the best season to visit Korea. Temperatures range from about 25°C (77°F) in September down to 3°C (37°F) by late November, with crisp air, low humidity, and colorful leaves (called danpung, 단풍) especially from mid-October to early November.

  • September: light layers are enough — cotton shirts and a thin cardigan for the evening.
  • October–November: long-sleeve tops, a sweater, and a light-to-medium jacket. Bring a slightly warmer jacket for late November, since it can turn cold quickly.
  • Comfortable walking shoes matter more than in any other season — this is peak hiking and leaf-viewing season, and popular spots involve a lot of walking.


Autumn foliage at Seoul Olympic Park. Photo: Ziggymaster, Wikimedia Commons, licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

Winter (December–February): genuinely cold, so dress for it

Korean winters are colder than many first-time visitors expect, especially from countries with mild winters. Average temperatures run from -5°C to 5°C (23–41°F), January and February are the coldest months, and snow is common — including sudden heavy snowfalls.

  • A heavy winter coat that covers your hips or longer, plus gloves, a scarf, and a warm hat.
  • Thermal base layers (thin, warm underlayers worn beneath your regular clothes) make a bigger difference than one extra thick sweater.
  • Boots with good grip — sidewalks can get icy, especially after snow melts and refreezes overnight.
  • Hand warmers (hotpack, 핫팩) — small disposable heat packs sold everywhere in convenience stores — are a very Korean way to stay warm; locals stick them inside gloves, pockets, or shoes.


A palace guard at Gyeongbokgung Palace in winter. Photo: Wikimedia Commons, licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

One local habit worth copying

Koreans dress in layers in every season except deep summer, rather than one heavy item — it's easier to adjust when you go from a heated (or air-conditioned) subway car to the street and back again dozens of times a day. Buildings in Korea tend to run very warm in winter and very cold with air-conditioning in summer, so a light layer you can add or remove matters more here than in many other countries.

💬 Not sure what season you're traveling in, or want a packing tip for a specific trip? Ask away in the comments!

Quick comparison: what to pack by season

Season Months Avg. Temp Must-pack items
Spring March–May 0–22°C (32–72°F) Layers, light jacket, small umbrella
Summer June–August 23–28°C (73–82°F) Breathable clothes, sturdy umbrella, sunscreen
Autumn September–November 3–25°C (37–77°F) Light layers, sweater, comfortable walking shoes
Winter December–February -5–5°C (23–41°F) Heavy coat, thermal layers, gloves, hand warmers
meta_description: Packing for Korea? A season-by-season guide to what first-time travelers should bring for rainy spring, humid summer, crisp autumn, and freezing winter days.
